title: Sega Maple Bus (Dreamcast peripheral bus)
summary: The Dreamcast's half-duplex peripheral bus: 5 V power with 3.3 V TTL signalling on two lines (SDCKA/SDCKB) that alternate clock and data every bit. The host runs ~2 Mbps and polls peripherals about every 16 ms.
body:
Maple is the bus behind every Dreamcast controller port. Physically it is five contacts (VCC +5V, SDCKA, SDCKB, sense, GND); electrically it is a half-duplex two-wire serial bus on SDCKA and SDCKB. The catch that surprises people: the console POWERS peripherals at 5 V but the two data lines SIGNAL at 3.3 V TTL, so a 3.3 V microcontroller can talk to it directly with no level shifting -- only the VCC rail is 5 V.

The encoding is unusual. There is no fixed baud and no dedicated clock line. Instead the two lines take turns: for one bit, line A is the clock and line B carries the data; for the next bit they swap, B clocks and A carries data. The receiver latches the data line on the clock line's falling edge. Both lines idle HIGH through weak pull-ups. Frames are bracketed by distinctive start and end patterns (one line pulsed while the other is held), so a decoder syncs on those patterns rather than on a bit rate.

Speeds: the host drives roughly 160 ns per phase (~2 Mbps); peripherals answer slower, around 250 ns per phase. The Dreamcast polls each port about every 16 ms (60 Hz), which conveniently lines up input sampling with the video frame. A controller is itself a Maple host to its own sub-devices (VMU, rumble pack) over the expansion 'LM bus'.

Building an adapter: because the protocol is bit-level and role-swapping, you don't use a UART or SPI block -- you bit-bang it with precise timing. On an RP2040 this is a natural fit for a PIO state machine running at 3.3 V straight onto the bus (the basis of usb2maple-style controller adapters). Data pins are typically assigned as consecutive GPIOs.

examples: One bit: line A = clock, line B = data. Next bit: line B = clock, line A = data. The data line is sampled on the clock line's falling edge -- there is no separate clock wire and no fixed baud.

RP2040 adapter: a PIO state machine bit-bangs Maple timing directly at 3.3 V, no level shifter. Reference projects: GP2040-CE Dreamcast, OrangeFox86 DreamcastControllerUsbPico. Assign the two data GPIOs consecutively.
gotchas: 3.3 V TTL signalling, not 5 V -- a 3.3 V MCU interfaces directly; only VCC is 5 V.
Not UART/SPI: the two lines swap clock/data roles each bit and sample on the clock's falling edge. You need bit-level timing (RP2040 PIO / FPGA), not a stock serial peripheral.
Both lines idle HIGH via weak pull-ups; the bus is half-duplex.
Frames are delimited by start/end patterns on the two lines, not by a baud rate -- a decoder must sync on those patterns.
